title: Different Debt: An Addition to the Technical Debt Dataset and a Demonstration Using Developer Personality
text:
## 1.1. Technical Debt

The metaphorical notion of technical debt (TD) was introduced by Ward Cunningham more than 30 years ago [1]. Despite slight variations in the exact definition of the term, there is a reasonable consensus on TD being a “collection of design or implementation constructs that are expedient in the short term, but set up a technical context that can make future changes more costly or impossible” [2]. Over time, despite its inherent limitations [3], the TD metaphor has gained acceptance and found widespread use in both academic and practitioner circles [4].

Researchers have identified different types of TD and made efforts to categorize them. [5], for example, identify eight different dimensions of TD, comprising code, design and architecture, operational processes, among others [5]. Relatedly, [6] and [7] each distinguish between 15 different types of TD, including, for example, design debt, code debt, test debt, and documentation debt [6,7].

By definition, TD comes with advantages and disadvantages. Reported advantages lie particularly in increased short-term developer velocity [8]. Reported disadvantages [9] are decreased long-term velocity [8], reduced developer morale and motivation [10,11,4], as well as lower code quality and increased uncertainty and risk [5].

Beyond conceptual considerations [3], qualitative studies [10], and surveys [9], researchers have increasingly become interested in performing large-scale quantitative studies on TD using data mined from software repositories [12,13,14,15].

## 1.2. The Technical Debt Dataset and its Limitations

To enable such studies of TD, [16] developed the “Technical Debt Dataset” (TDD) [16]. It is a dataset of TD (primarily code debt) in various Apache Software Foundation (ASF) projects written in Java. It has been used in a variety of studies on TD [12,13,14,15]. In its most recent version 2.0, it contains a comprehensive analysis of the main branches of 31 projects. Aside from data obtained from PyDriller, Refactoring Miner, Jira, and Ptidej, the dataset most notably includes TD information generated using SonarQube.

Importantly, SonarQube requires the build of a commit to complete before it can provide TD information. For various reasons (e.g., deficient code or missing dependencies), however, builds may fail. Consequently, the TDD does not contain complete information for such commits. According to our own analyses, the SonarQube analyses were incomplete for more than 60% of commits in the covered projects.

Recent research has found that this is particularly problematic in cases where differences in TD between commits are of interest, because then missing information in either the focal commit or its parent commit leads to missing data in the ultimate analysis. This problem has been reported to reduce the size of samples dramatically, potentially impacting the validity of analyses performed on them. For instance, in the recent study on developer personality and TD by [17], the authors collected personality data for 121 developers who made commits that are within the scope of the TDD, but they could only use data from 19 developers due to missing TD information in the TDD [17].

Further, it is well-known that TD detection tools may come to different assessments of TD [18]. As the TDD only contains TD items from SonarQube, it is thus naturally limited in this way, too.
